lessons.title: Shared Flats, Rent to a Spouse and Other Grey Areas

body.text: Grey areas in HRA are not loopholes. The law answers almost every one of them with the same three questions: who actually paid the rent, for which home, and where did the money end up? Get those right and most grey areas turn clear.

children.text: The first two chapters assumed one employee, one flat and one landlord. Real life in Indian cities is messier. Three friends split a 3BHK in Koramangala. A working couple in Pune shares one rent. A husband pays rent to his wife for a flat she owns. A fresher in Noida lives in a PG with meals included. This lesson works through each of these, using the rules you already know.
Shared Flats: Claim Your Share, Not the Whole Rent

When flatmates share a home, each person can claim HRA exemption only on the rent they actually bear. It does not matter whose name is on the agreement or who presses "pay" on the landlord's UPI ID, as long as the money trail shows each person's share.

Aakash, Rohit and Karan rent a ₹60,000 3BHK in Koramangala, Bengaluru. Aakash pays the landlord the full ₹60,000 every month, and the other two transfer ₹20,000 each back to him. Aakash's basic is ₹60,000 and his HRA is ₹30,000 a month.

body.title: Aakash's claim: his share vs the full rent

columns.label: Wrong: the full ₹60,000 he transfers
points: His flatmates' transfers back to him expose the overclaim

cells: Put all flatmates on the rent agreement, or get the landlord to acknowledge each person's share in writing
Links each person to the home and to their share of rent
Ideally, each person pays their share directly to the landlord
Creates a clean, separate money trail for each claim
If one person pays the landlord, others transfer their share to that person by bank or UPI every month, never in cash
Proves who really bore how much
Each person declares only their share in Form 124 and in their return
Prevents the same rupee of rent being claimed twice
Each person gives the landlord's PAN if their own share exceeds ₹1,00,000 a year
The PAN threshold applies to the rent you pay, not the total for the flat

children.text: A married couple renting one home follows the same rule as flatmates: each spouse claims only what they actually pay. Both cannot claim the full rent. What many couples miss is that the split they choose, if it is genuine, changes the family's total exemption.
Vikram and Neha rent a ₹50,000 flat in Kharadi, Pune. Vikram's basic is ₹1,00,000 and HRA ₹50,000. Neha's basic is ₹60,000 and HRA ₹30,000. Both are on the old regime.

body.caption: Same flat, same rent, three genuine payment patterns (annual)

cells: Each pays ₹25,000 from their own account
Vikram pays the full ₹50,000
Neha pays the full ₹50,000

body.title: Family exempt HRA by who pays the rent

body.text: The split must follow real payments, not a spreadsheet. If Neha transfers ₹25,000 to Vikram every month and Vikram then claims the full rent, the bank records show he bore only half. Decide who pays first, set up the transfers that way, and claim accordingly. Also compare slab rates: exempting more HRA in the higher-slab spouse's hands saves more tax.

body.title: Scenario: Changing the Split
body.scenario: Vikram is in the 30% slab and Neha in the 20% slab. They currently split the rent 50:50. A friend suggests Vikram should pay all the rent from April, while Neha takes over groceries, utilities and the car EMI of roughly the same amount.
body.prompt: Is this allowed, and roughly what does it do to their combined tax?
body.modelAnswer: It is allowed, provided Vikram genuinely pays the full rent from his own account and Neha genuinely pays the other household costs from hers. HRA law does not dictate how a couple divides expenses. Under the 50:50 split, Vikram exempts ₹1,80,000 (saving about ₹56,160 at 30% plus cess) and Neha exempts ₹2,28,000 (about ₹47,424 at 20% plus cess), roughly ₹1,03,584 in total. If Vikram pays everything, he exempts ₹4,80,000, saving about ₹1,49,760, and Neha's exemption falls to nil. The family saves roughly ₹46,176 more a year, assuming both stay in the same slabs. What would not be allowed is Vikram claiming the full rent while Neha still sends him half of it.

children.text: This is the grey area people ask about most. The Income-tax Act does not prohibit it, and tribunals have allowed genuine arrangements. In Bajrang Prasad Ramdharani v. ACIT (ITAT Ahmedabad, 2013), exemption was allowed on rent paid to the assessee's wife, supported by receipts and bank transfers. In Abhay Kumar Mittal v. DCIT (ITAT Delhi, 8 February 2022), the tribunal held there is no legal bar on paying rent to one's wife and allowed the claim.

body.title: Case file: Abhay Kumar Mittal v. DCIT

cells: Rent paid
₹5,34,000 to his wife from September 2012 to March 2013
Ownership
The flat was owned by his wife
The officer's concern
How his wife could afford the flat, since he had funded ₹87.5 lakh of the purchase
Wife's own funds
The balance came from her own sources, including matured fixed deposits
Tribunal's view
No legal bar on paying rent to a spouse. There was also no bar on him funding his wife from his known income. The claim was allowed

children.text: Rent to a spouse needs everything that rent to a parent needs from Lesson 9: sole ownership by the spouse, a written agreement, bank transfers and the spouse declaring the rent. It also carries two catches specific to marriage.

cells: You transferred the house to your spouse without adequate consideration
For tax, you can be treated as the deemed owner of a house you gift to your spouse
You may be treated as living in your own house, so the HRA tests fail
Your spouse bought the house with money you gifted
Clubbing provisions under Section 99 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Section 64 of the 1961 Act) can add income from assets funded by a gift to your spouse back into your income
The rent may be taxed in your hands anyway, so the family saves nothing and the arrangement looks artificial
The flat is jointly owned by both of you
You would be paying rent partly to yourself
The claim is weak at best, and fails for your own share

body.text: Form 124 now asks for your relationship with the landlord, so a rent-to-spouse claim will be visible to your employer and, through the landlord PAN, to the tax department. The arrangements that survive are the ones where the spouse genuinely owns the home with their own money, and the rent is genuinely paid and taxed.

body.caption: Grey areas and how to handle them

cells: PG or co-living where rent includes meals
Only the accommodation part is rent. Food, laundry and housekeeping are not
Ask the operator for an invoice that separates accommodation from services, and claim only the accommodation amount
Society maintenance charges
Counts as rent if it is part of the rent paid to the landlord under the agreement
If you pay the society directly on top of rent, keep it out of your claim unless the agreement treats it as rent
Furnished flat with one consolidated rent
Generally treated as rent for the accommodation
Avoid a separate furniture hire agreement unless it is genuinely separate
Rent paid in advance for several months
Counts for the months it covers, not the month you paid it
Allocate it across the period, especially if it crosses 31 March
Rent paid in cash
Legally allowed, but hard to prove
Switch to bank transfer or UPI. If cash is unavoidable, keep signed receipts for every month and proof of cash withdrawals
Landlord lives abroad (NRI)
HRA can still be claimed
You have a TDS obligation on rent paid to a non-resident. Lesson 16 covers TDS on rent

body.title: Quick Check: The PG Invoice
body.question: Tara pays ₹18,000 a month to a co-living operator in Noida. The invoice shows ₹11,000 for the room and ₹7,000 for meals, housekeeping and Wi-Fi. What rent should she use for her HRA calculation?
options: ₹18,000, because she pays it all to the same operator
₹7,000, because services are the taxable part
Nothing, because a PG is not a house
body.explanation: HRA exemption is for rent on residential accommodation. The room charge of ₹11,000 qualifies. Meals, housekeeping and Wi-Fi are services, not rent. A PG or co-living room is still residential accommodation, so the exemption is available on the accommodation part.

body.title: Try It: Tara's Exemption
body.prompt: Tara's basic salary is ₹35,000 a month and her HRA is ₹14,000 a month. Noida is a 40% city. Using only the ₹11,000 monthly accommodation charge as rent, what is her annual exempt HRA? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Salary ₹4,20,000. Limit 1: ₹1,68,000. Limit 2: ₹1,32,000 minus ₹42,000 = ₹90,000. Limit 3: 40% of ₹4,20,000 = ₹1,68,000. The smallest is Limit 2, so ₹90,000 is exempt. Had she used the full ₹18,000, she would have claimed ₹1,68,000, overstating her exemption by ₹78,000.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Clubbing Rule
body.textWithBlank: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, income from assets you transfer to your spouse without adequate consideration can be added back to your income under Section ___, which replaced Section 64 of the 1961 Act.
body.explanation: Section 99 carries forward the clubbing provisions of Section 64. It is why rent paid to a spouse who bought the home with money you gifted may not save the family any tax.

body.title: Grey Area Health Check
steps: If you share a flat, confirm your claim uses only your own share of rent, backed by bank transfers
If you rent with your spouse, decide who pays what, pay it that way from separate accounts, and claim only what each of you pays
If you pay rent to your spouse, confirm they solely own the home, bought it with their own money or a documented loan, and declare the rent
If you live in a PG or co-living space, get an invoice that separates the room charge from services
Remove deposits, brokerage, separately billed maintenance and utility bills from your rent figure
Replace any cash rent with bank transfers or UPI from next month

cards.definition: The share of rent you paid from your own money. In a shared flat or couple's home, this is the only amount you can claim.
ITAT Delhi, 8 February 2022. Held there is no legal bar on claiming HRA exemption for rent paid to a spouse, and allowed a genuine claim.
A person treated as owner for tax purposes, for example when they transfer a house to their spouse without adequate consideration.
Income from assets transferred to a spouse without adequate consideration can be taxed in the transferor's hands. Replaced Section 64 of the 1961 Act.
The part of a PG or co-living charge that pays for the room. Meals and services are excluded from rent.

points: Flatmates and couples can each claim HRA only on the rent they actually bear, backed by a clear money trail
A genuine choice about which spouse pays rent can change the family's total exemption and tax
Rent to a spouse is not banned. Tribunals have allowed genuine claims, including Abhay Kumar Mittal v. DCIT in 2022
Watch the spouse-specific catches: deemed ownership of a gifted house and clubbing of income from gifted money under Section 99
In a PG or co-living space, only the accommodation charge counts as rent
Deposits, brokerage, separately billed maintenance and utilities are not rent, and cash rent is legal but hard to defend
